Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: A friend who has just started assembling furniture asks for a quick video call because the instructions are confusing.
Situation2: A patient with a chronic autoimmune disease requires a very specific and ongoing treatment plan.
Story:
My phone buzzed just as I was reviewing the latest lab results for Mrs. Kim, my patient with lupus. Her case was complicated, and I needed to double-check her medication dosages before sending the prescription to the pharmacy. The message was from Alex, my oldest friend. “SOS! Can you hop on a quick video call? I’m drowning in screws and Swedish instructions.” I could almost hear the panic in his text. He’d just moved into his new apartment, and I’d promised to help him settle in, but I hadn’t expected it to be today.

I stared at the two screens—one with Alex’s desperate face waiting for a call, the other with Mrs. Kim’s chart and a blinking cursor. Alex needed me to be the friend who drops everything, the one who makes him laugh when he’s frustrated. But Mrs. Kim depended on me to be precise, focused, and thorough. If I rushed her prescription, I could make a dangerous mistake. My chest tightened as I weighed the pull of loyalty against the gravity of responsibility, feeling the pressure of both worlds closing in, demanding I choose.
